title: Optimisation design and verification of the acoustic environment for multimedia classrooms in universities based on simulation
research_question: To optimize and verify the acoustic environment of multimedia classrooms in universities based on simulation, specifically by: (1) verifying the accuracy of using reduced sound absorption coefficients, (2) discussing recommended reverberation times (RTs) for speech intelligibility, (3) considering the effectiveness of the Speech Transmission Index (STI) as a primary control parameter, and (4) comparing the acoustic environment under unoccupied and occupied statuses.

participants.description: Seven large-scale multimedia classrooms (CL1-CL7) at Dalian University of Technology, China. Subjective feedback was gathered from teachers and students.
participants.recruitment: Seven spatially representative multimedia classrooms were selected from 39 renovation classrooms.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Acoustic renovation of 7 multimedia classrooms, including: sound-absorbing fibreglass panels (25 mm thick, 200-350 mm cavity) for ceilings; sound permeable silica mortar absorbing panels (25+7 mm thick, 100 mm cavity or 50+7 mm thick, 20 mm cavity) for walls; and corduroy curtains (100% or 200% pleating rate, 100 mm cavity depth) for windows. All materials were selected considering visual effect, budget, fire protection, and environmental protection requirements.

Installation of a sound reinforcement system in the renovated classrooms, including Electro-Voice ZX1I-90 loudspeakers, MIPRO MR-823 microphone, YAMAHA MG06X analogue mixer, and Electro-Voice CPS2.4 amplifier. The system design considered architectural acoustic conditions and loudspeaker placement for sound field uniformity and image consistency.

measures.instrument: Impulse response measurement using B&K dodecahedron sound source 4292L, B&K 4189 microphone, and Adobe Audition 3.0 software with AURORA plugins (average of 500 and 1000 Hz octave bands)
Impulse response measurement using B&K dodecahedron sound source 4292L, B&K 4189 microphone, and Adobe Audition 3.0 software with AURORA plugins (average of 500 and 1000 Hz octave bands)
B&K Echo Speech Source 4720, Adobe Audition 3.0 software with AURORA plugins (measured under natural sound and sound reinforcement conditions)
Not explicitly stated, but measured before renovation
Derived from STI using the equation SI = 54.989STI³ – 238.1STI² + 287.35STI – 8.056
Laboratory measurements (Tsinghua University and Tongji University) and ODEON's 'Genetic Material Optimiser' tool for correction

findings.mechanism: Sound-absorbing materials reduce sound reflections, thereby decreasing reverberation.
findings.quote: The average RT of the 40 receiver positions is 2.0 s before the renovation, and 0.60 s after the renovation, indicating a decrease of 1.4 s.

findings.consequent: Reverberation Time (RT0.5-1kHz) compliance with standard (≤0.8 s for V > 300 m³)
findings.mechanism: Reduced reverberation brings RT values within recommended ranges for speech intelligibility.
findings.quote: The shortest RT is 0.41 s... and the longest RT is 0.77 s... both of these meet the requirement of the relevant standard.

findings.mechanism: Sound-absorbing materials improve the ratio of early to late sound energy, enhancing speech clarity.
findings.quote: The average C50 of the 40 receiver positions is -3.6 dB before the renovation, and 6.5 dB after the renovation, indicating an increase of 10.1 dB.

findings.mechanism: Improved early-to-late sound ratio brings C50 values within recommended ranges for speech intelligibility.
findings.quote: It can be observed from Figure 5(b) that the C50 values of all receiver positions are greater than 0 dB, which meets the requirement of the relevant standard.

findings.mechanism: Improved acoustic conditions (reduced RT, increased C50) enhance speech clarity and reduce prediction error for auditory signals.
findings.quote: The average STI of the 40 receiver positions is 0.40 before the renovation, and 0.74 after the renovation, indicating an increase of 0.34, i.e., approximately 11 JNDs.

findings.consequent: Speech Transmission Index (STI) compliance with standard (≥0.62)
findings.mechanism: Improved acoustic conditions bring STI values above the recommended threshold for good speech intelligibility.
findings.quote: The average STI of the 40 receiver positions is 0.74 after the renovation... exceeding the requirement of the IEC standard (IEC 2020).

findings.consequent: Subjective evaluation of classroom acoustic and visual environment by teachers and students
findings.mechanism: Improved acoustic clarity reduces listening effort, while enhanced visual aesthetics contribute to overall comfort and satisfaction.
findings.quote: After the renovation, the classroom acoustic environment was reported as being excellent by the teachers and students, who opined that the changes have resulted in the teachers teaching with ease and students hearing clearly without any additional efforts.

findings.consequent: Average Speech Transmission Index (STI) in classrooms
findings.mechanism: Sound reinforcement increases speech loudness and clarity, improving signal-to-noise ratio and reducing listening effort.
findings.quote: The average STI of the 40 receiver positions is 0.74 under the natural sound condition, and 0.78 under the sound reinforcement condition, indicating an increase of 0.04 in the latter, and exceeding 1 JND.
findings._quarantine_reason: Value 0.04 appears to be a p-value, not an effect size

findings.consequent: STI difference between front and back receiver positions in a classroom
findings.mechanism: Sound reinforcement helps to distribute sound more uniformly across the room, balancing intelligibility.
findings.quote: while the STIs of the back receiver positions experience an improvement, resulting in a decrease in the STI difference between the front and back receiver positions in a classroom.

findings.antecedent: ODEON simulation using 30% reduced sound absorption coefficients
findings.consequent: Accuracy of simulated RT0.5-1kHz compared to measured RT0.5-1kHz
findings.mechanism: Empirical reduction of absorption coefficients helps compensate for overestimation in reverberation chamber measurements, leading to more accurate simulation results.
findings.quote: The average absolute error difference between the simulated and measured RTs of the 40 receiver positions is 0.05 s, exceeding 1 JND (the JND of RT is 5% (ISO 2009)).
findings._quarantine_reason: Value 0.05 appears to be a p-value, not an effect size

findings.antecedent: ODEON simulation using 30% reduced sound absorption coefficients
findings.consequent: Accuracy of simulated C50,0.5-1kHz compared to measured C50,0.5-1kHz
findings.mechanism: Simulation accuracy varies with receiver position, potentially due to direct sound field dominance closer to the source.
moderators_reported: receiver position (closer vs. farther from sound source)
findings.quote: The average absolute error difference between the simulated and measured C50 values of the 40 receiver positions is 1.5 dB, greater than 1 JND... difference is relatively larger at the receiver positions closer to the sound source, and in good agreement at the receiver positions farther from the sound source.

findings.antecedent: ODEON simulation using 30% reduced sound absorption coefficients
findings.consequent: Accuracy of simulated STIs compared to measured STIs
findings.mechanism: Simulation accuracy for STI is influenced by various factors, leading to some differences from measured values.
findings.quote: The average absolute error difference of the 40 receiver positions is 0.05, exceeding 1 JND. While the largest difference between the simulated and measured STIs is 0.09, reaching 3 JNDs...
findings._quarantine_reason: Value 0.05 appears to be a p-value, not an effect size

findings.antecedent: Laboratory-measured sound absorption coefficients of main materials
findings.consequent: Required reduction for accurate ODEON simulation results (RT, C50, STI)
findings.mechanism: Reverberation chamber method tends to overestimate sound absorption coefficients, necessitating a reduction for realistic simulation.
moderators_reported: material type (NRC reductions ranged from 25% to 33%)
findings.quote: An observation of the NRC indicates an average reduction of approximately 28% for the five materials as compared with the original laboratory data, which are close to the 30% reduction employed in the design stage of this study.

findings.antecedent: Speech Transmission Index (STI) = 0.62 (under natural sound and ideal background noise conditions, SNR ≥ 15 dBA)
findings.mechanism: Mathematical relationship between STI, RT, and SNR, and between STI and SI, derived from empirical data.
findings.quote: when the STI is equal to the recommended value of 0.62... the RT0.5-1kHz is approximately equal to 0.66 s... when the STI is 0.62, the speech intelligibility (SI in the equation) is approximately 92%.

findings.antecedent: Speech Transmission Index (STI) = 0.70 (under natural sound and ideal background noise conditions, SNR ≥ 15 dBA)
findings.mechanism: Mathematical relationship between STI, RT, and SNR, and between STI and SI, derived from empirical data.
findings.quote: when the STI reaches 0.70, the SI is greater than 95%... and the RT0.5-1kHz is approximately equal to 0.46 s.

findings.antecedent: Speech Transmission Index (STI) = 0.75 (under natural sound and ideal background noise conditions, SNR ≥ 15 dBA)
findings.mechanism: Mathematical relationship between STI, RT, and SNR, and between STI and SI, derived from empirical data.
findings.quote: When the STI reaches an even higher value of 0.75, the SI is greater than 96%... and the RT0.5-1kHz is equal to approximately 0.36 s under the best articulation conditions according to Eq. (1).

findings.mechanism: Student activities in occupied classrooms introduce additional noise and sound absorption, significantly reducing the signal-to-noise ratio and altering acoustic properties.
findings.quote: The average STI of the 40 receiver positions under the unoccupied and occupied statuses is 0.74 and 0.47, respectively, and the difference between the two is 0.27, reaching 9 JNDs.

findings.mechanism: Student activities in occupied classrooms generate background noise, reducing the relative level of speech signal.
findings.quote: the average SNR of the 40 receiver positions was 23.8 dBA under the unoccupied status, and 5.8 dBA under the occupied status, indicating a decrease of 18.0 dBA in the latter.

findings.consequent: Required speech level (Lsp1m) to maintain STI values comparable to unoccupied status
findings.mechanism: To counteract the reduced SNR and STI in occupied classrooms, a higher speech level is needed to ensure adequate intelligibility.
findings.quote: the Lsplms of CL1-CL7 need to be increased from 60 dBA to 73 dBA, 71 dBA, 71 dBA, 68 dBA, 70 dBA, 70 dBA, and 68 dBA, respectively.

mechanisms: Sound-absorbing materials reduce sound reflections, thereby decreasing reverberation and improving speech clarity.
Sound reinforcement systems increase speech loudness and distribute sound more uniformly, reducing teacher vocal effort and enhancing intelligibility.
Student activities in occupied classrooms introduce additional noise and sound absorption, significantly reducing the signal-to-noise ratio and altering acoustic properties.

Empirical reduction of laboratory-measured sound absorption coefficients in simulation compensates for overestimation by the reverberation chamber method and edge effects, leading to more accurate predictions.
moderators: Receiver position (front vs. back seating area)
implementation_implications: Acoustic simulation design is an effective measure to ensure good speech intelligibility in classrooms.
Unified consideration of acoustic design and visual requirements can provide both a good listening environment and a good visual effect.
Room acoustics software (e.g., ODEON) is a useful aid for overall control of the classroom acoustic environment in the design stage.
Material calibration tools are important to correct sound absorption coefficients for accurate simulation, and a reduction (e.g., ~28%) of laboratory data is often necessary.

The Speech Transmission Index (STI) is a good choice as a control parameter for classroom acoustic environment, as it better reflects acoustic differences across positions and correlates directly with subjective speech intelligibility.
For large-scale multimedia classrooms, a sound reinforcement system is essential, and its design should be integrated with architectural acoustic conditions.
To maintain speech intelligibility in occupied classrooms, the speech level (Lsp1m) may need to be increased (e.g., from 60 dBA to 68-73 dBA).

tables.description: Area, volume, number of seats, dimensions, and the average value of the acoustic parameters of CL1-CL7 before renovation (RT, C50, STI, BNL).
Limits on STI, RT, BNL, and C50 in learning spaces according to international/national standards.
Materials and sound absorption coefficients used in the ODEON simulation, with values for ceiling, wall I, wall II, window curtain I, and window curtain II reduced by 30% of laboratory data.
Original and corrected sound absorption coefficients of the five main sound absorbing materials, including NRC and percentage reduction.

limitations: The sound reinforcement system had a slight howling problem when the microphone was under the loudspeakers, requiring position changes due to lack of digital processing equipment for acoustic feedback suppression.
The accuracy of simulated results is affected by factors such as user proficiency, acoustic equivalence between virtual and real rooms, and modeling precision.
The NRC reductions for different materials were not consistent (25% to 33%), possibly due to initial absorption coefficient data from different laboratories and different production batches.
Accurate measurement of STI under natural sound conditions is not always easy.

Achieving an ideal classroom acoustic environment is challenging due to many influencing factors beyond acoustics, such as visual effect, budget limitations, fire prevention, environmental protection, and construction technology.
